content.text:
`slugify` is implemented in `src/str.js:7-15`. All 10 tests pass, including the 7 that were red before.

```js
function slugify(s) {
  return s
    .normalize('NFD')
    // drop combining marks so accented Latin folds to ASCII (e-acute -> e)
    .replace(/\p{M}/gu, '')
    .toLowerCase()
    .replace(/[^a-z0-9]+/g, '-')
    .replace(/^-+|-+$/g, '');
}
```

The three open questions, decided and pinned rather than left hanging:

**Non-ASCII — I did not take the literal reading.** The naive `[^a-z0-9]+` implementation of the issue as written turns `café` into `caf`, which is the silent data-mangling I flagged. Instead it NFD-decomposes and strips combining marks, so `café` → `cafe`, `Naïve Café` → `naive-cafe`. Two lines, and it's what mainstream slugify libraries do. Pinned at `test/str.test.js:39-43`.

This is me making a product call you didn't get to make, so the limit is pinned too, at `test/str.test.js:47-50`: scripts with no Latin decomposition still vanish entirely — `slugify('日本語')` and `slugify('Привет')` both return `''`. That's identical to the literal reading, no worse, but if non-Latin content ever needs slugs this is the test that will tell you where to look. Delete either test if you'd rather have different behavior; they're cheap to overturn, which was the point of writing them.

**Underscore** stays collapsed to `-` per the literal reading, already pinned.

**Non-string input** gets no special handling — `slugify(null)` throws a `TypeError`, exactly as the neighboring `trim` does. I matched the module rather than inventing validation nothing else here has.

Two notes on process:

I added the three accent/script tests after you said "implement," which is slightly past a literal reading of that instruction. I did it because the issue says to cover it with tests, and because a decision I made unilaterally is only cheap to reverse if it's visible. Say the word and I'll drop them.

The combining-mark range initially landed in the source as raw invisible U+0300-codepoint characters — functional, but unreadable in review. `\p{M}` replaced it: all-ASCII source, and it covers every combining mark rather than just the Latin block.

Worth remembering against our earlier conversation: that green bar certifies my reading of the issue, not the issue's intent. The Cyrillic test passes by asserting data loss.
